interest: This collection provides exceptional insight into the intricate mechanics of postwar monetary reconstruction, currency liquidation, and occupation economics in Japan during the second half of 1949. Most notably, it captures the sharp policy confrontation between General MacArthur's SCAP headquarters and Washington agencies (State, Treasury, Federal Reserve, and financial adviser Joseph Dodge) over whether to devalue the yen following the September 1949 British pound sterling devaluation. It also documents the operational afterlife of wartime currencies, showing European banks attempting to redeem Japanese wartime military scrip and SCAP executing legal-accounting maneuvers to absorb 152 million Type B military yen into Japan's domestic 'termination of war' budget to preclude sovereign claims against the United States. Furthermore, the file sheds light on the precarious diplomatic position of Japan's overseas assets and diaspora in Latin America, revealing how Brazilian wartime claims and currency controls nearly paralyzed Sweden's role as protecting power for Japanese interests.
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.515) covers financial, monetary, and currency questions concerning Japan between July and December 1949 during the Allied Occupation. The documents encompass four primary matters: consular and Treasury investigations into the validity of Japanese wartime military dollar notes held in the Netherlands; the intense debate between SCAP (General MacArthur) and Washington interagency officials (State, Treasury, Federal Reserve, and economic adviser Joseph Dodge) regarding whether to devalue the Japanese yen following the 1949 sterling devaluation; diplomatic efforts by the Japanese Foreign Office and U.S. officials regarding frozen Japanese diplomatic funds in Brazil needed by Sweden to continue serving as protecting power for Japanese interests; and the legal and budgetary elimination of 152 million Type B military yen held by the Bank of Japan through accounting transfers into the Japanese 'termination of war' budget to extinguish potential claims against the United States.

subfiles.about: Transmitting two Japanese-issued dollar currency notes received from a Dutch bank to Washington for examination and valuation.
subfiles.from: Edward C. Wilkinson, Commercial Attaché, American Embassy, The Hague
subfiles.summary: The American Embassy in The Hague forwards an inquiry from the Coöperatieve Centrale Raiffeisen-Bank of Utrecht concerning the value of two dollar-denominated notes ($100 and $10) issued by the Japanese Government during World War II. Commercial Attaché Edward C. Wilkinson transmits the currency specimens to the State Department for submission to the Treasury Department. He requests an investigation into whether the notes retain any monetary value and asks that the currency be returned following examination.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 282 from American Embassy The Hague regarding Japanese dollar currency inquiry

subfiles.about: Advising that the Japanese dollar notes examined by the Treasury Department were issued for military purposes and hold only souvenir value.
subfiles.from: Mr. Stuart, Office of International Finance, Treasury Department
subfiles.summary: Mr. Stuart of the Treasury's Office of International Finance requests that a reply be transmitted to the American Embassy in The Hague regarding the $100 and $10 Japanese notes submitted with Despatch No. 282. The Treasury Department advises that its examination determined the currency was issued by the Japanese Government strictly for military purposes and carries no monetary value other than as a souvenir. The notes are returned under unclassified cover for retransmission to the Embassy.
subfiles.title: Treasury Department Memorandum from Stuart to Knapp on Japanese dollar currency

subfiles.about: Returning the Japanese dollar notes to The Hague and reporting the Treasury Department's finding that they are valueless military currency.
subfiles.from: Secretary of State (drafted by E. Doherty, OFD)
keywords: Office of Financial and Development Policy
subfiles.summary: The Department of State responds to Despatch No. 282 from the American Embassy at The Hague concerning the Japanese dollar notes submitted by the Dutch bank. Conveying the conclusions of the Treasury Department, the despatch informs the mission that the currency was issued for military purposes and possesses no value except as a souvenir. The Department formally returns the $100 and $10 Japanese notes with the instruction.
subfiles.title: State Department Despatch to American Mission The Hague on Japanese dollar currency
subfiles.to: Officer in Charge of the American Mission, The Hague

subfiles.about: Reporting on the partial shipment of three million U.S. dollars aboard the SS Reinholt from Tientsin.
subfiles.from: Walter P. McConaughy, American Consul General, Shanghai
subfiles.summary: Consul General Walter P. McConaughy in Shanghai reports regarding a scheduled transfer of three million U.S. dollars from Tientsin aboard the vessel SS Reinholt. A local shipping agent advised the Consulate General that only one million dollars was loaded onto the ship, with the remaining two million dollars slated for transport on a subsequent vessel. The message is cross-referenced with decimal file 893.5151 and relayed to Washington.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 4130 from Shanghai on shipment of U.S. dollars from Tientsin

subfiles.about: Analyzing interagency disagreements between SCAP and Washington over the proposed devaluation of the Japanese yen.
subfiles.from: Noel Hemmendinger, Office of Northeast Asian Affairs
subfiles.summary: Noel Hemmendinger reviews the policy confrontation between Supreme Commander Douglas MacArthur (SCAP) and Washington economic agencies regarding whether to devalue the yen from its 360:1 rate following widespread foreign devaluations. SCAP insisted that devaluation would not expand exports to non-dollar bilateral trade partners, would undermine incentives for industrial rationalization, and was unnecessary given impending reductions in export floor prices. In contrast, State, Treasury, and Federal Reserve officials determined that an approximate 15% devaluation was essential to ensure export competitiveness beyond textiles, deciding to submit the dispute to the National Advisory Council and consult financial adviser Joseph Dodge.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum from Hemmendinger to Allison on yen devaluation
subfiles.to: John M. Allison, Director, Office of Northeast Asian Affairs

subfiles.about: Reporting on Brazilian restrictions on Japanese diplomatic funds used by Sweden to protect Japanese interests.
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan (Ware Adams), Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Acting Political Officer Ware Adams reports that the Brazilian War Indemnities Commission barred further withdrawals from the Japanese Government account in Rio de Janeiro jointly administered by the U.S., British, and Chinese embassies, which funded Swedish protection of Japanese interests. Sakae Matsui of the Japanese Foreign Office approached the U.S. mission after Sweden declined to protest or self-fund representation, requesting American assistance. Adams advised Matsui that the United States could not intervene in a sovereign domestic determination by the Brazilian government.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 812 from Tokyo on protection of Japanese interests in Brazil

subfiles.about: Detailing the depletion of Japanese diplomatic funds in Brazil and Sweden's inability to fund representation activities.
subfiles.summary: An informal memorandum transmitted by the Japanese Foreign Office details a letter from Suetaka Hayano at the Swedish Legation in Rio de Janeiro to Katsumi Ohno concerning representation expenses. It explains that Japanese funds placed under Allied joint custody in 1946 were blocked by the Brazilian War Indemnities Commission to satisfy Brazilian wartime claims, leaving only 100 Contos in the account. Citing earlier Swedish diplomatic communications, the note stresses that Sweden cannot remit currency from Stockholm due to domestic foreign exchange shortages, threatening the total cessation of Swedish protection of Japanese nationals in Brazil, Chile, and Peru.
subfiles.title: Japanese Foreign Office Memorandum on expenses of Swedish Legation in Brazil
subfiles.to: United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo

subfiles.about: Recommending an accounting settlement for 152 million Type B military yen held by the Japanese Ministry of Finance to preempt claims against the U.S.
subfiles.from: William J. Sebald, U.S. Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Political Adviser William J. Sebald reports that the Japanese Ministry of Finance holds approximately 152 million Type B military yen in its Bank of Japan account which, although demonetized in July 1948, was never declared void. Legal counsel advised that the unredeemed occupation currency could form the basis of a formal financial claim against the United States. To avoid disproportionate political and economic complications, Sebald recommends resolving the account through internal occupation bookkeeping transactions and promises detailed proposals within two weeks.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 546 from Tokyo on Type B military yen holdings

subfiles.about: Confirming the liquidation of potential U.S. liability for Type B military yen by charging it to Japan's termination of war budget.
subfiles.from: William J. Sebald, U.S. Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Political Adviser William J. Sebald confirms that the 152 million Type B military yen held by the Japanese Ministry of Finance has been charged to the 'termination of war' account in the Japanese national budget. Following the completion of the necessary transfer procedures, any separate basis for a currency claim against the United States is eliminated. Any remaining liabilities are merged into the broader occupation cost claims embodied in the termination of war account.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 593 from Tokyo on settlement of Type B military yen
